questions.prompt: You dust the shelf to clean it. What are you doing?
questions.explanation: In this cleaning instruction, dust means taking the particles away.

questions.prompt: A wheel is stuck fast. What does fast mean here?
questions.explanation: Stuck fast describes something held firmly. The surrounding words tell you which meaning fits.

questions.prompt: Why is bat, meaning an animal or sporting equipment, not a contronym?
options: Its meanings are different, but not opposites
All words with two meanings are contronyms
questions.explanation: A contronym has opposing meanings. An animal and a piece of sporting equipment are different things, not opposite meanings.

title: Contronyms: when a word means its own opposite

sources.name: Merriam-Webster — Words that are their own opposites

practice: Ready to look at familiar clues in a different way? Try Connections.

sections.html:
A contronym is a word with opposing meanings. You can dust a shelf to remove particles, then dust dough with flour to add them. Same instruction, opposite jobs.

Also called Janus words, these words usually make sense once you read the whole sentence. Merriam-Webster explains the idea.
sections.title: One instruction, two very different jobs

sections.html:
The dictionary lists both meanings of dust. Compare:

  • Dust the model spaceship. Take the dust away.
  • Dust the dough with flour. Add a light coating.

If someone simply points at a kitchen counter and says “dust it”, asking a follow-up question seems fair.
sections.title: Dust: put it on or take it off?

sections.html:
A cyclist moving fast is quick. A wheel stuck fast is firmly fixed. The dictionary includes both senses, but the surrounding phrase matters.

Different meanings alone are not enough: an animal bat and a cricket bat are different things, not opposites.
sections.title: Fast can move—or stay firmly put

sections.html: No. A contronym has opposing meanings. Homophones share a sound: flour and flower do not mean opposite things. Try our flour-or-flower examples if those labels feel tangled.
sections.title: Is that the same as a homophone?

sections.html:
“The runner moved fast, but the gate was held fast by a rusty bolt.” Which use describes movement?

Show the answer

The runner moves quickly. The gate stays firmly in place.
